clue.text: A jolly girl at sea

parts.note: a jolly is old slang for a Royal Marine, abbreviated RM
Ada is a girl's name

explanation.surface: A cheerful young woman is out on a sea voyage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'jolly' looks like an adjective for the girl, but it is a noun: a Royal Marine. The definition is loose: a fleet of warships is what one finds at sea.
explanation.definitionFit: A great fleet of warships is something found sailing out on the ocean.

clue.text: Old citadel's ploughed soil sustaining a season's yield

indicators.note: in a down clue the jumbled soil sits beneath and holds up the crop

parts.note: a crop is the harvest of a season

indicators.note: ploughed earth is turned over, so the letters of soil are rearranged

explanation.surface: The ancient fortress's tilled earth supports a year's harvest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ploughed' turns SOIL into OLIS, which 'sustaining' places under A CROP in this down answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The Acropolis of Athens is the classic example of an ancient Greek hilltop fortress.

clue.text: Battleground spy captured by scholar

indicators.note: the spy is held inside the scholar's letters

parts.note: an MA, Master of Arts, is a scholar
an agent is a spy

explanation.surface: On a battlefield a spy is caught by an academic.
explanation.definitionFit: Magenta in northern Italy was the site of an 1859 battle, which gave the dye its name.

clue.text: Translucent material for mixed-up Idahoans

indicators.note: mixed means the letters are blended into a new order

explanation.surface: Sheer fabric is wanted for some confused people from Idaho.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mixed-up' reads as one adjective, but 'up' is part of the anagram fodder with IDAHOANS; 'material for' only links.
explanation.definitionFit: Diaphanous fabric is so fine and light that it lets light through.

clue.text: Like a Shakespearian fairy describing an intended trap?

explanation.surface: Someone compares a person to a fairy from Shakespeare, or describes a snare being set.
explanation.walkthrough: Cobweb is one of Titania's fairies in A Midsummer Night's Dream; the second reading treats a spider's web as a trap meant for flies.
explanation.definitionFit: Cobweb is a fairy attendant in A Midsummer Night's Dream, and a spider's web is the snare a spider lays for flies.

clue.text: Terrible thing done at the front, suddenly

indicators.note: the word for done is placed first, before the jumbled letters

parts.note: over means finished, done

indicators.note: terrible suggests the letters are in a dreadful mess

explanation.surface: Something awful has been carried out ahead of the lines, without warning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Terrible' makes NIGHT; 'done' looks like part of the surface's deed but is the finished sense, and 'at the front' places it first.
explanation.definitionFit: An overnight success happens abruptly, as if in a single night.

clue.text: Better half of poem in Welsh and English

indicators.note: the poem's title goes inside the two abbreviations

parts.note: If is Rudyard Kipling's famous poem

explanation.surface: A married man's partner features in a verse in two languages.
explanation.walkthrough: 'If—' is Kipling's well-known poem of advice to a son.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Better half' is a jocular idiom for one's spouse.

clue.text: Weep in pub upset spree

indicators.note: the word for weep goes inside the overturned pub
in a down clue upset means turned upside down, read bottom to top

parts.note: taken as written
to ooze is to seep or weep, as a wound does

explanation.surface: Crying in a pub after an overturned drinking session.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down answer 'upset' reads the pub upwards, giving BUP; the drink-fuelled surface hides that 'Weep' is a verb of seeping.
explanation.definitionFit: A booze-up is a drinking session, a bout of heavy drinking.

clue.text: Bumpkin's bond with student

parts.note: a yoke is a tie or bond
L for learner stands for a student

explanation.surface: A country lad's tie to a learner.
explanation.definitionFit: A yokel is an unsophisticated rustic, a country hick.

clue.text: In the East, a real luminary

indicators.note: in shows the letters are found within the words of the phrase that follows

explanation.surface: A true celebrity arises in the Orient.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across 'East, a real', from inside East to the start of real.
explanation.definitionFit: A luminary is a famous person, a celebrity in their field.

clue.text: Surrounded by soldiers, granny is holding sway

indicators.note: the word for granny sits within the word for soldiers, which surround it

parts.note: REGT is the abbreviation for regiment, a body of soldiers
nan is a familiar word for a grandmother

explanation.surface: A grandmother hemmed in by troops nevertheless keeps control.
explanation.definitionFit: Regnant describes a monarch who reigns in their own right, exercising power and rule.

clue.text: Hirsute feature of the Spanish crowd

parts.note: el is the Spanish word for 'the'
a flock is a crowd of people or animals

explanation.surface: A hairy characteristic is spotted among a Spanish throng.
explanation.definitionFit: An elflock is a tangled lock of hair, supposedly knotted by elves, so a hairy feature.

clue.text: Stupefied 28 employed by old magazine

indicators.note: the drinker's word comes after the magazine's name, as if working for it

parts.note: Punch was a long-running British humorous weekly magazine
28 across is TIPPLER; a drinker of that kind is drunk

explanation.surface: A dazed drinker works for a defunct magazine.
explanation.walkthrough: The cross-reference points to the answer at 28, a drinker, giving DRUNK. Punch was a famous British satirical magazine, closed in 2002.
explanation.definitionFit: Punch-drunk means dazed or confused, like a boxer after too many blows to the head.

clue.text: Descended rapidly from the hill

explanation.surface: Someone tumbled quickly down a slope.
explanation.definitionFit: To fall is to drop suddenly, past tense here; a fell is a hill or moor in northern England.

clue.text: Willing to ring an estate employee

parts.note: game means willing, as in 'game for anything'
a keeper is a ring worn to hold a wedding ring in place

explanation.surface: Someone is happy to telephone a worker on a country estate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ring' suggests a phone call, but a keeper ring guards a wedding ring.
explanation.definitionFit: A gamekeeper looks after game birds and animals on a country estate.

clue.text: Erudite king comes to a sad end

parts.note: King Lear is Shakespeare's tragic monarch

indicators.note: sad is read as 'in a sorry state', so the letters of end are jumbled

explanation.surface: A scholarly monarch meets a tragic finish, as Lear did.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sad' gives NED; the surface fits Shakespeare's Lear, whose story ends in tragedy.
explanation.definitionFit: Erudite and learned are synonyms, both meaning showing great scholarship.

clue.text: The libertine Hecuba destroyed in the river

indicators.note: the jumbled queen's name goes inside the river

parts.note: the Dee is a river of Wales, England and Scotland

indicators.note: destroyed means the letters are broken apart and rearranged

explanation.surface: A rake ruins Hecuba, Troy's queen, in the river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'destroyed' gives BAUCHE. Hecuba was Queen of Troy, so the surface reads like a tale of Trojan ruin.
explanation.definitionFit: A debauchee is a dissolute person given to sensual indulgence.

clue.text: Man holding racket is a heavy breather

indicators.note: the man's name holds the word for racket inside it

parts.note: Gus is a man's name
a ramp is slang for a swindle or racket

explanation.surface: A fellow gripping a tennis racket is puffing hard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'racket' suggests tennis but means a swindle, RAMP.
explanation.definitionFit: The grampus, a kind of dolphin or killer whale, is famed for its loud blowing, as in 'puff like a grampus'.

clue.text: Reliable soldiers will in the end capture many a rascal

indicators.note: the word for reliable takes the letter for many inside it

parts.note: sound means dependable, reliable
C is the Roman numeral for a hundred, many
RE is the Royal Engineers, a body of soldiers

indicators.note: in the end takes the final letter of will

explanation.surface: Dependable troops will eventually catch plenty of villains.
explanation.walkthrough: 'capture' puts the hundred after the first letter of the reliable word; the surface reads as soldiers rounding up villains.
explanation.definitionFit: A scoundrel is a dishonest rogue, a villain.

clue.text: Rejected American doctor constrains posh cricket club to give way

indicators.note: the outer letters hold the posh and club letters inside them
rejected means the American abbreviation is turned back to front

parts.note: U means upper-class, posh
MB is a medical degree, Bachelor of Medicine

explanation.surface: An American doctor who was turned away keeps a smart cricket club from yielding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rejected' gives SU; 'constrains' puts the posh and club letters just after its first letter, inside SUMB.
explanation.definitionFit: To succumb is to yield or surrender, to stop resisting.

clue.text: Purchase obtained from this old hag supervising a counter

indicators.note: in a down clue supervising puts the hag on top, over the counter

parts.note: crow is slang for an ugly old woman
a bar is a counter where drinks are served

explanation.surface: Someone buys from a crone who runs a shop counter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Purchase' means leverage, not buying.
explanation.definitionFit: A crowbar is a lever, giving purchase, the mechanical grip needed to prise something open.

clue.text: It gives the lutenist no bother in new composition

indicators.note: the letters are composed afresh, put into a new order

parts.note: no is nought, the letter O

explanation.surface: A lute player has no trouble with a newly written piece.
explanation.walkthrough: 'no' gives O; with BOTHER the letters are rearranged. The definition calls the instrument what supplies the lutenist's music.
explanation.definitionFit: The theorbo is a large bass lute of the Baroque era, an instrument a lute player performs on.

clue.text: It isn't fully radical, by the sound of it

definitions.text: It isn't fully radical, by the sound of it

parts.words: It isn't fully radical, by the sound of it
parts.note: radical puns on root; a small root with the diminutive suffix -let sounds like a root that is let off from being a full one

explanation.surface: Something seems only partly revolutionary.
explanation.walkthrough: 'radical' means of the root; the diminutive ending makes a root that is less than full-sized.
explanation.definitionFit: A rootlet is a small subsidiary root branching from a larger one.

clue.text: Boat at the front taking prisoner across river

parts.note: P is an abbreviation for prisoner
to row is to take a boat across a river

explanation.surface: A boat at the head of the line takes a captive over the water.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boat' tempts as the definition alone, but the whole phrase means the front part of a boat.
explanation.definitionFit: The prow is the forward part of a ship's hull, its bow.

clue.text: He learns to put up with cheek at university

indicators.note: in a down clue put up means the letters are read upwards

parts.note: lip is cheek, insolence
up means in residence at university

explanation.surface: A student tolerates insolence while at college.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put up with' reads as tolerate, but 'put up' reverses LIP and UP together in this down answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A pupil is a student, someone being taught.

clue.text: An acrobat may do it and be ruined

explanation.surface: A gymnast performs a fall and is wrecked.
explanation.definitionFit: An acrobat may tumble down as part of a routine; tumbledown also describes a building falling to pieces, dilapidated.

clue.text: Grouse-shooter's stand is an object of ridicule

explanation.surface: A hunter's hide becomes a laughing stock.
explanation.definitionFit: A butt is a screen behind which shooters wait for grouse on a moor, and a target of jokes.

clue.text: Thelonious' brother?

parts.note: the jazz pianist Thelonious bore a surname that is also a word for a religious brother

explanation.definitionFit: A brother in a religious order is a friar, and the jazz pianist Thelonious had that surname.

clue.text: Piped music from a holy tower in Scotland

parts.note: pi is slang for pious, holy
a broch is an ancient round stone tower found in Scotland

explanation.surface: Bagpipe music drifts down from a sacred Scottish tower.
explanation.definitionFit: A pibroch is a set of variations for the Highland bagpipe, music played on pipes.

clue.text: Drinker — one learning to drive in a truck

indicators.note: the learner's letter goes inside the truck's name

parts.note: a tipper is a truck whose body tips to unload
L is the learner plate on a British car

explanation.surface: A drunk learner driver is at the wheel of a lorry.
explanation.walkthrough: L-plates mark a learner driver in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: A tippler is someone who habitually drinks alcohol.

clue.text: Bird appears to like centre of forest abnormally

indicators.note: abnormally means the letters are arranged in an irregular way
the middle two letters of forest are taken

explanation.surface: A bird seems fond of the heart of the woodland in an odd way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'centre of' takes RE from forest; with TO and LIKE these are rearranged by 'abnormally'.
explanation.definitionFit: The lorikeet is a small brightly coloured parrot of Australasia.

clue.text: Ruthless gangster seen by Republican in bar

indicators.note: the Republican letter sits inside the word for bar

parts.note: but means except, as does bar
Al Capone was the notorious Chicago gangster

explanation.surface: A violent mobster is spotted drinking with a Republican politician in a pub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bar' suggests a pub but means except, BUT.
explanation.definitionFit: Brutal means savagely cruel, without pity.
